pos: n. (Athenian philosopher, c. 470–399 BC, executed by his own city for impiety and corrupting the youth)
etymology: Greek Sokrates. He wrote nothing; what survives is Plato's and Xenophon's report of him. Calvin cites him as the best the pagan world produced, and uses him to mark the limit of that world.
biblical_def: Socrates is not named in Scripture; his city and his method are. Paul met the philosophers of Athens in the market daily as Socrates had (Act 17:17–18), and was accused, as Socrates was, of setting forth strange gods. Scripture grants the pagan mind a real light: “that which may be known of God is manifest in them; for God hath shewed it unto them” (Rom 1:19). It also names where that light stops: “professing themselves to be wise, they became fools” (Rom 1:22); “the world by wisdom knew not God” (1Co 1:21). And it puts the true starting point elsewhere: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom” (Pro 9:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Socratic as pertaining to Socrates, his philosophy or method of teaching; the Socratic method being that of teaching by a series of questions and inductions.
webster_full: SOCRATIC, SOCRATICAL, a. Pertaining to Socrates, the Grecian sage, or to his manner of teaching and philosophizing.
The Socratic method of reasoning and instruction was by questions, the answers to which led on the disputant to the conclusion sought.
SOCRATISM, n. The doctrines or philosophy of Socrates.
scriptures: Then certain philosophers of the Epicureans, and of the Stoicks, encountered him. And some said, What will this babbler say? other some, He seemeth to be a setter forth of strange gods: because he preached unto them Jesus, and the resurrection.
Rom 1:19
Because that which may be known of God is manifest in them; for God hath shewed it unto them.
Rom 1:22
Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools,
For after that in the wisdom of God the world by wisdom knew not God, it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe.
Pro 9:10
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: and the knowledge of the holy is understanding.
corruption_summary: The best pagan is made into an honorary Christian, or dismissed as though he saw nothing at all.
corruption_paragraphs: Socrates is the standing test case for the doctrine of common grace, and the church has erred in both directions about him. Some of the fathers made him a Christian before Christ; some of the Reformers' successors would allow him nothing. The Reformed position holds two things at once. He genuinely saw something — that the unexamined life is not worth living, that it is better to suffer wrong than to do it, that a man's soul is what he ought to care for — and Romans 1:19 says such sight is not accidental, since God shewed it unto them. That is common grace, and it is God's gift whoever receives it.

The limit is equally firm and it is not that his ethics were poor. Romans 1:22 does not say they became foolish in their reasoning; it says professing themselves to be wise, they became fools, and the folly named in the following verses is worship misdirected. A man may reason beautifully about the good and still not know whom to thank, and 1 Corinthians 1:21 states the outcome as a settled fact of history: after all of it, the world by wisdom knew not God. The failure was not intellectual capacity but a knowledge that requires being told.

Proverbs 9:10 puts the two together with a word that does the work: the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom. Not its capstone, added after the philosophy is finished, but the point from which understanding starts. Which is why a Christian may read Socrates with real profit and must not read him as a preparation that the gospel then completes. Athens produced the finest questions the unaided mind has asked. It did not produce the answer, and Paul had to bring it to them.
roots_summary: Greek sophia (G4678), wisdom; moraino (G3471), to become foolish; Hebrew yirath YHWH (H3374), the fear of the LORD; reshith (H7225), beginning.
roots_lines: Hebrew yirath YHWH reshith chokmah (H3374, H7225) — the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom; Proverbs 9:10, 1:7, Psalm 111:10.
Greek emoranthesan (G3471) — they became fools; Romans 1:22.
Greek dia tes sophias (G4678) — by wisdom; 1 Corinthians 1:21.
usage: “That which may be known of God is manifest in them” — and he saw some of it.
“Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools” — not in reasoning, in worship.
“The beginning of wisdom” — the beginning, not the capstone.

pos: n. pl. (a fourth-century North African party holding that sacraments administered by unworthy ministers are invalid, and that the church must consist of the pure)
etymology: From Donatus, their bishop at Carthage. The schism began over bishops who had handed over the Scriptures during Diocletian's persecution; Augustine wrote against them for thirty years.
biblical_def: The Donatists held that a church containing the unworthy is no church, and that a minister's sin voids his ministry. The Lord's own parables give a mixed field until the harvest: “Nay; lest while ye gather up the tares, ye root up also the wheat with them. Let both grow together until the harvest” (Mat 13:29–30); and a net that “gathered of every kind”, sorted only when it is full (Mat 13:47–48). Paul allows a mixed house: “in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and of silver, but also of wood and of earth” (2Ti 2:20). And the efficacy rests elsewhere: “shall their unbelief make the faith of God without effect? God forbid” (Rom 3:3), for “other foundation can no man lay” (1Co 3:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Donatists as a sect of ancient heretics who held that their sect alone constituted the true church, and rebaptized those who joined them from other churches.
webster_full: DONATIST, n. One of a sect in Africa, followers of Donatus, in the fourth century.
The Donatists held that theirs was the only true church, that baptism and ordination by any other were void, and rebaptized all who came over to them.
scriptures: But he said, Nay; lest while ye gather up the tares, ye root up also the wheat with them.
Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto a net, that was cast into the sea, and gathered of every kind:
But in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and of silver, but also of wood and of earth; and some to honour, and some to dishonour.
Rom 3:3
For what if some did not believe? shall their unbelief make the faith of God without effect?
For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ.
corruption_summary: The demand for a pure church is a good instinct turned into a doctrine, and it ends by making every believer's comfort depend on his minister's secret life.
corruption_paragraphs: The Donatists were not cynics; they were the party of the martyrs, appalled that bishops who had surrendered the Scriptures under torture were back in their pulpits. The instinct is right, and the church that feels nothing at such a thing is worse off than they were. What went wrong was the inference: if the minister is defiled, the sacrament he administers is void. Follow that and no believer can ever be sure of his baptism, since he cannot know what the man who baptised him was privately. Augustine's answer was that the sacrament's validity rests on Christ, not on the hand that holds the cup — which is why Rome, Geneva and the Baptists have all refused to rebaptize on the ground of a minister's later disgrace.

The parables settle the ecclesiology and their tone is worth noticing. The servants' proposal in Matthew 13:28 is entirely reasonable — wilt thou that we go and gather them up? — and the householder refuses, not because the tares are harmless but because the wheat would go with them. That is a statement about the limits of human discernment. A church can and must discipline visible, provable sin; it cannot sort hearts, and the attempt has cost more wheat than it ever removed of tares.

The corruption recurs whenever a movement makes its own purity the mark of the true church, and it has a predictable career: rigorous separation, then separation from the separated, then a remnant certain it alone is the body of Christ. Second Timothy 2:20 is unglamorous and freeing — a great house has vessels of wood and earth in it, and the same passage tells a man to purge himself, which is the only purging Scripture assigns him with certainty. The visible church is mixed until the harvest, and this is a mercy, since most of us would not have survived an earlier sorting.
roots_summary: Greek zizanion (G2215), tares; sagene (G4522), a dragnet; skeuos (G4632), a vessel; apistia (G570), unbelief.
roots_lines: Greek zizanion (G2215) — tares, darnel; Matthew 13:25–40.
Greek sagene (G4522) — a dragnet; Matthew 13:47 only — it gathered of every kind.
Greek skeuos (G4632) — vessel; 2 Timothy 2:20–21, Romans 9:21–23, Acts 9:15.
usage: “Let both grow together until the harvest” — and the servants' proposal was reasonable.
“Vessels of wood and of earth” — in a great house, by design.
“Shall their unbelief make the faith of God without effect?” — God forbid.

pos: adj. (tending to stir up rebellion against lawful authority)
etymology: Latin seditio, from sed-, apart, and itio, a going — a going apart, a faction. The AV has the word at Ezra 4:15, of Jerusalem in the Persian correspondence.
biblical_def: Seditious conduct stirs up rebellion. The charge is laid against Jerusalem in a letter to Artaxerxes: it is “a rebellious city, and hurtful unto kings and provinces, and that they have moved sedition within the same of old time” (Ezr 4:15). It is laid falsely against Christ: “We found this fellow perverting the nation, and forbidding to give tribute to Caesar” (Luk 23:2), and against Paul: “a pestilent fellow, and a mover of sedition among all the Jews throughout the world” (Act 24:5). The Christian's rule is submission: “Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers… whosoever therefore resisteth the power, resisteth the ordinance of God” (Rom 13:1–2), with one boundary: “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines seditious as pertaining to sedition; partaking of the nature of sedition; tending to excite commotion against government; disposed to excite violent or concerted opposition to lawful authority.
webster_full: SEDITIOUS, a. Pertaining to sedition; partaking of the nature of sedition; as seditious behavior; seditious strife.
2. Tending to excite sedition; as seditious words.
3. Disposed to excite violent or concerted opposition to lawful authority; turbulent; factious.
SEDITION, n. A factious commotion of the people, a tumultuous assembly of men rising in opposition to law or the administration of justice.
scriptures: Ezr 4:15

That search may be made in the book of the records of thy fathers: so shalt thou find in the book of the records, and know that this city is a rebellious city, and hurtful unto kings and provinces, and that they have moved sedition within the same of old time: for which cause was this city destroyed. moved: Cald.
Luk 23:2
And they began to accuse him, saying, We found this fellow perverting the nation, and forbidding to give tribute to Caesar, saying that he himself is Christ a King.
Act 24:5
For we have found this man a pestilent fellow, and a mover of sedition among all the Jews throughout the world, and a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes:
Rom 13:1
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.
Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
corruption_summary: The charge is laid against faithful men by hostile authorities, and Romans 13 is quoted to silence them.
corruption_paragraphs: Both Christ and Paul were formally charged with sedition, and both charges were false. That is the first thing to hold, because it establishes that being accused of subversion is not evidence of it — and the accusers in Luke 23 were themselves the ones stirring the crowd. The Lord had in fact answered the tribute question by telling them to render unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's, which is the opposite of what they reported. Governments and religious establishments have always found the sedition charge convenient against men whose real offence is a rival loyalty.

Romans 13 is nonetheless meant, and Paul wrote it under Nero. Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers — not the godly powers, not the powers one voted for. Taxes are to be paid, honour rendered, magistrates recognised as ministers of God for good. Christians who chafe at this because their government is unjust should notice whose government Paul had in mind, and that Peter says the same thing (submit yourselves… honour the king) while the same emperor was in office.

The boundary is exactly one clause wide and it is not elastic. Acts 5:29 is spoken by men who had been ordered by the lawful council to stop preaching Christ: We ought to obey God rather than men — and they then submitted to the beating rather than resisting it. That is the Reformed shape of civil disobedience: refusal at the precise point of the sinful command, no wider, and acceptance of the penalty. It is neither the quietism that obeys everything nor the sedition the church is so often accused of, and it is much harder than either.
roots_summary: Greek stasis (G4714), sedition, insurrection; diastrepho (G1294), to pervert, turn aside; hupotasso (G5293), to be subject; Hebrew marad (H4775), to rebel.
roots_lines: Greek stasis (G4714) — sedition, insurrection; Acts 24:5, Luke 23:19, Mark 15:7, Acts 19:40.
Greek hupotasso (G5293) — to be subject, submit; Romans 13:1, 13:5, 1 Peter 2:13, Titus 3:1.
Hebrew marad (H4775) — to rebel; Ezra 4:12, 4:15, 4:19, Nehemiah 2:19.
usage: “We found this fellow perverting the nation” — a false charge, from the men stirring the crowd.
“Let every soul be subject” — written under Nero.
“We ought to obey God rather than men” — and then they took the beating.

pos: n. (the power of speaking well; oratory that moves as well as informs)
etymology: Latin eloquentia, from eloqui, to speak out. Scripture has an eloquent preacher (Apollos), an inarticulate one (Moses), and one who deliberately declined the art (Paul).
biblical_def: Eloquence is skill in speech. Scripture presents it three ways and blesses none of them absolutely. Apollos “an eloquent man, and mighty in the scriptures, came to Ephesus” and was still taught “the way of God more perfectly” by a tentmaker and his wife (Act 18:24–26). Moses pleads the opposite: “O my Lord, I am not eloquent… but I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue” (Exo 4:10), and is sent anyway. Paul declines the art on purpose: “I, brethren, when I came to you, came not with excellency of speech or of wisdom” (1Co 2:1), because the gospel is not preached “with wisdom of words, lest the cross of Christ should be made of none effect” (1Co 1:17). His critics said “his speech contemptible” (2Co 10:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines eloquence as oratory; the art or the act of speaking with fluency, elegance and force, so as to please, affect and persuade.
webster_full: ELOQUENCE, n. Oratory; the art or the act of speaking with fluency, elegance and force, so as to please, affect and persuade.
Eloquence is not merely the power of speaking well, but of speaking so as to command attention, to move the passions, and to persuade the will.
ELOQUENT, a. Having the power of oratory; speaking with fluency, propriety, elegance and animation.
scriptures: And a certain Jew named Apollos, born at Alexandria, an eloquent man, and mighty in the scriptures, came to Ephesus.
Exo 4:10
And Moses said unto the LORD, O my Lord, I am not eloquent, neither heretofore, nor since thou hast spoken unto thy servant: but I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue.
And I, brethren, when I came to you, came not with excellency of speech or of wisdom, declaring unto you the testimony of God.
For Christ sent me not to baptize, but to preach the gospel: not with wisdom of words, lest the cross of Christ should be made of none effect.
For his letters, say they, are weighty and powerful; but his bodily presence is weak, and his speech contemptible.
corruption_summary: The gift is treated as the qualification for ministry, and Paul refused to use his and Moses did not have one.
corruption_paragraphs: First Corinthians 1:17 gives the reason for the refusal and it is a reason about causation, not taste: not with wisdom of words, lest the cross of Christ should be made of none effect. Eloquence can produce every visible sign of a work of God — tears, decisions, a full room, a moved congregation — without the Spirit doing anything, and that is its danger. A church cannot easily tell, from the outside, whether it was persuaded or converted, and neither can the man in the pulpit. Paul's remedy was to remove the variable.

It does not follow that plainness is a virtue in itself, and Scripture will not support the preacher who mistakes being dull for being faithful. God gave Apollos his gifts, Luke commends them, and the same Apollos watered where Paul planted. The book of Isaiah is magnificent prose, the Psalms are poetry, and the Lord's parables are the most memorable short fiction ever composed. The question is what the skill is serving. Eloquence spent on making the text clear and its weight felt is a gift returned; eloquence spent on making the speaker admired is what Corinth was buying.

Exodus 4 is the encouragement for the other kind of man, and God's answer to Moses is worth reading exactly: Who hath made man's mouth?… have not I the LORD? Now therefore go, and I will be with thy mouth, and teach thee what thou shalt say. He does not grant the excuse and He does not supply eloquence; He supplies Himself. Moses remained slow of speech and led a nation out of Egypt, and the words he eventually wrote have outlasted every orator of the ancient world.
roots_summary: Greek logios (G3052), eloquent, learned; huperoche logou (G5247, G3056), excellency of speech; sophia logou (G4678), wisdom of words; Hebrew kebad peh (H3515, H6310), heavy of mouth.
roots_lines: Greek logios (G3052) — eloquent, learned; Acts 18:24 only.
Greek sophia logou (G4678 with G3056) — wisdom of words; 1 Corinthians 1:17, 2:1, 2:4.
Hebrew kebad peh ukebad lashon (H3515) — slow of speech and of a slow tongue; Exodus 4:10.
usage: “Lest the cross of Christ should be made of none effect” — the reason for the refusal.
“I am not eloquent” — and he was sent anyway.
“His speech contemptible” — said of Paul, by Corinthians.

pos: n. (the office of a bishop or overseer; in the AV, the office Judas vacated)
etymology: Old English bisceoprice, from bishop and rice, dominion. The AV uses it once, quoting Psalm 109:8 of Judas: “his bishoprick let another take” (Act 1:20).
biblical_def: A bishopric is the office of oversight. Peter applies the psalm to the vacancy Judas left: “his bishoprick let another take” (Act 1:20). It is a work rather than a rank: “If a man desire the office of a bishop, he desireth a good work” (1Ti 3:1), and the qualifications that follow are character, not credentials: “a bishop must be blameless, as the steward of God” (Tit 1:7). The same men are called elders and told to “feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood” (Act 20:28). Peter defines the manner: “Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly” (1Pe 5:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines bishopric as a diocese; the district over which the jurisdiction of a bishop extends; and the charge of instructing and governing in spiritual concerns; office.
webster_full: BISHOPRIC, n. A diocese; the district over which the jurisdiction of a bishop extends.
2. The charge of instructing and governing in spiritual concerns; office.
BISHOP, n. An overseer; a spiritual superintendent, ruler or director; applied to Christ.
Ye were as sheep going astray, but are now returned to the Shepherd and Bishop of your souls. 1 Pet. ii.
scriptures: Act 1:20
For it is written in the book of Psalms, Let his habitation be desolate, and let no man dwell therein: and his bishoprick let another take.
This is a true saying, If a man desire the office of a bishop, he desireth a good work.
Tit 1:7
For a bishop must be blameless, as the steward of God; not selfwilled, not soon angry, not given to wine, no striker, not given to filthy lucre;
Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind;
corruption_summary: A bishopric becomes a territory to govern, and the New Testament makes it a flock to feed.
corruption_paragraphs: The English word carries a history the Greek does not. Episkopos is a compound of over and see — one who watches — and in the New Testament it names the same men as presbuteros, elder: Paul calls for the elders of the Ephesian church and then tells those same men the Holy Ghost has made them overseers. Titus 1 does it in two verses, appointing elders and then giving the qualifications of a bishop. Whatever a church concludes about its polity, it cannot get a rank above the eldership out of these texts, because the words are used of one office.

First Timothy 3:1 gives the right ambition and the right description in one line: if a man desire the office of a bishop, he desireth a good work. Not a good position — a good work, and the list that follows is almost entirely about how a man lives: blameless, sober, given to hospitality, not greedy of filthy lucre, ruling his own house well, having a good report of them which are without. Only one item, apt to teach, is a competence at all. A church selecting officers by gift, presence or professional attainment is using a different list from the one Paul supplied.

First Peter 5 names the three temptations of the office and each is still current: by constraint rather than willingly, for filthy lucre rather than of a ready mind, and as lords over God's heritage rather than as ensamples to the flock. Set against that is the title Peter gives Christ in the same letter — the Shepherd and Bishop of your souls — which settles who the office belongs to. Every human bishopric is a sub-oversight under a chief Shepherd who shall appear, and the crown of glory in verse 4 is what a man is working for, not a diocese.
roots_summary: Greek episkope (G1984), oversight, the office of a bishop; episkopos (G1985), overseer; presbuteros (G4245), elder; poimaino (G4165), to shepherd, feed.
roots_lines: Greek episkope (G1984) — oversight, bishopric; Acts 1:20, 1 Timothy 3:1, and of visitation, Luke 19:44, 1 Peter 2:12.
Greek episkopos (G1985) — overseer, bishop; Acts 20:28, Philippians 1:1, 1 Timothy 3:2, Titus 1:7, 1 Peter 2:25.
Greek poimaino (G4165) — to shepherd, tend; Acts 20:28, 1 Peter 5:2, John 21:16.
usage: “His bishoprick let another take” — the AV's one use, and it is Judas's.
“He desireth a good work” — a work, not a position.
“The Shepherd and Bishop of your souls” — whose office it finally is.

pos: n. (the crime of swearing falsely; a false oath taken in God's name)
etymology: Latin perjurium, from per-, through or amiss, and jus, right — a swearing amiss. The AV has perjured persons at 1 Timothy 1:10.
biblical_def: Perjury is a false oath, and it profanes the name invoked to guarantee it. The Law joins the two: “ye shall not swear by my name falsely, neither shalt thou profane the name of thy God” (Lev 19:12). The Ninth Commandment forbids it in court: “Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour” (Exo 20:16). Zechariah's flying roll goes out against the thief and “him that sweareth falsely by my name”, and remains in his house to consume it (Zec 5:4). Paul lists “perjured persons” among those the law is made for (1Ti 1:10). And Peter, denying his Lord, “began he to curse and to swear, saying, I know not the man” (Mat 26:74).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines perjury as the act or crime of wilfully making a false oath, when lawfully administered; false swearing.
webster_full: PERJURY, n. The act or crime of wilfully making a false oath, when lawfully administered; or a crime committed when a lawful oath is administered by some person authorized, to a person who swears wilfully, absolutely and falsely, in a matter material to the issue.
PERJURE, v.t. To forswear; to swear falsely.
PERJURED, a. Guilty of perjury; having sworn falsely.
scriptures: And ye shall not swear by my name falsely, neither shalt thou profane the name of thy God: I am the LORD.
Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour.
Zec 5:4

I will bring it forth, saith the LORD of hosts, and it shall enter into the house of the thief, and into the house of him that sweareth falsely by my name: and it shall remain in the midst of his house, and shall consume it with the timber thereof and the stones thereof.
For whoremongers, for them that defile themselves with mankind, for menstealers, for liars, for perjured persons, and if there be any other thing that is contrary to sound doctrine;
Then began he to curse and to swear, saying, I know not the man. And immediately the cock crew.
corruption_summary: Perjury is filed as a courtroom offence, and Scripture treats it first as a sin against God's name.
corruption_paragraphs: Leviticus 19:12 puts the two clauses in the order that explains the gravity: ye shall not swear by my name falsely, neither shalt thou profane the name of thy God. The second clause is not an additional prohibition; it is what the first amounts to. An oath calls God as witness and guarantor, so a false oath enlists Him in a lie, which is why the Third Commandment and the Ninth meet here. The damage to the neighbour is real and it is the lesser half; the offence is against the One whose name was used as collateral.

Zechariah's vision is the strangest treatment of the subject in Scripture and its detail is precise. A flying roll twenty cubits by ten goes out over the face of the whole earth against the thief and against him that sweareth falsely, and it shall remain in the midst of his house, and shall consume it with the timber thereof and the stones thereof. The curse does not strike and depart; it takes up residence. That is a picture of a sin that eats a household from inside over years, and any lawyer or pastor who has watched a family built on a sustained lie will recognise the mechanism.

Matthew 26:74 keeps the doctrine from being applied only to other people. Peter, under no legal oath and in no court, curses and swears that he does not know the man — and the account is in the Gospel because Peter told it. That is the honesty of the New Testament about its own leadership. The relevant thing for the reader is what follows: he went out and wept bitterly, and was restored by a threefold question on a beach. The perjurer is not beyond mercy, and the man who preached at Pentecost had sworn falsely about Christ seven weeks earlier.
roots_summary: Hebrew shaqar (H8267), falsehood; shava shav (H7650, H7723), to swear in vain; Greek epiorkos (G1965), a perjurer; anathematizo (G332), to curse oneself under oath.
roots_lines: Hebrew lashaqer (H8267) — falsely; Leviticus 19:12, Jeremiah 5:2, 7:9, Zechariah 5:4.
Greek epiorkos (G1965) — perjured person; 1 Timothy 1:10 only; the verb epiorkeo, Matthew 5:33.
Greek katanathematizo (G2653) — to curse oneself, invoke a curse; Matthew 26:74.
usage: “Neither shalt thou profane the name of thy God” — which is what the false oath amounts to.
“It shall remain in the midst of his house” — the curse takes up residence.
“Began he to curse and to swear” — and Peter told the story himself.

pos: n. (deception practised under a false character; a fraud passed off as genuine)
etymology: Latin impostura, from imponere, to lay upon — to impose upon a man is to lay a false thing on him. The religious impostor is the one Scripture warns of most.
biblical_def: An imposture is a fraud wearing a true character's clothes. The Lord's warning is of counterfeits good enough to test the elect: “there shall arise false Christs, and false prophets, and shall shew great signs and wonders; insomuch that, if it were possible, they shall deceive the very elect” (Mat 24:24). Paul says the last one comes with real power: “whose coming is after the working of Satan with all power and signs and lying wonders” (2Th 2:9). Simon the sorcerer bewitched Samaria, “giving out that himself was some great one” (Act 8:9). And the imitation reaches to the apostolate itself: “such are false apostles, deceitful workers, transforming themselves into the apostles of Christ… for Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light” (2Co 11:13–14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines imposture as deception practised under a false or assumed character; fraud or imposition practised by a false pretender.
webster_full: IMPOSTURE, n. Deception practiced under a false or assumed character; fraud or imposition practiced by a false pretender.
IMPOSTOR, n. One who imposes on others; a person who assumes a character for the purpose of deception; a deceiver under a false character.
scriptures: For there shall arise false Christs, and false prophets, and shall shew great signs and wonders; insomuch that, if it were possible, they shall deceive the very elect.
Even him, whose coming is after the working of Satan with all power and signs and lying wonders,
Act 8:9
But there was a certain man, called Simon, which beforetime in the same city used sorcery, and bewitched the people of Samaria, giving out that himself was some great one:
For such are false apostles, deceitful workers, transforming themselves into the apostles of Christ.
And no marvel; for Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light.
corruption_summary: Power and signs are treated as proof, and Scripture says the impostor will have both.
corruption_paragraphs: The single most important thing in these texts is that the counterfeit works. The Lord does not say the false Christs will fail to produce signs; He says they shall shew great signs and wonders. Paul does not say the man of sin will be unconvincing; he says his coming is with all power and signs and lying wonders. A church that authenticates a ministry by results, power or the extraordinary has adopted a test that Scripture explicitly says the enemy can pass, and has left itself with nothing to fall back on when the results arrive.

The test Scripture does give is doctrinal and moral, and it is duller. Try the spirits whether they are of God, and the trial in 1 John is a confession about Christ come in the flesh. Test the prophet by whether he speaks according to the law and the testimony. Know them by their fruits — and the fruits in Matthew 7 are set against a defence built entirely on works of power: many will say, have we not prophesied in thy name, and in thy name cast out devils, and in thy name done many wonderful works? The answer is I never knew you, and the works are not disputed.

Second Corinthians 11:14 supplies the reason the counterfeit is so good: Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light. Not into a monster. The imposture is always toward the attractive, the reverent, the impressively spiritual, which is why the men Paul is describing were out-preaching him at Corinth and looked more apostolic than he did. His own credentials, listed in the following verses, are stripes, imprisonments, shipwrecks and the care of the churches — an anti-résumé, and the only one an impostor would never think to forge.
roots_summary: Greek pseudochristos (G5580), false Christ; terata pseudous (G5059), lying wonders; metaschematizo (G3345), to transform, disguise; planao (G4105), to lead astray.
roots_lines: Greek pseudochristoi / pseudoprophetai (G5580, G5578) — false Christs and false prophets; Matthew 24:24, Mark 13:22.
Greek metaschematizo (G3345) — to change appearance, disguise; 2 Corinthians 11:13–15, Philippians 3:21.
Greek terasin pseudous (G5059, G5579) — lying wonders; 2 Thessalonians 2:9.
usage: “Shall shew great signs and wonders” — great ones, not failed ones.
“Transformed into an angel of light” — toward the attractive, never the monstrous.
“I never knew you” — and the works are not disputed.

pos: adj. (not genuine; counterfeit; of illegitimate birth)
etymology: Latin spurius, of illegitimate birth. The two senses meet in Hebrews 12:8, where those without chastening are called bastards, and not sons — a spurious sonship.
biblical_def: A spurious thing has the form without the descent. Hebrews applies it to sonship: if ye be without chastisement, “whereof all are partakers, then are ye bastards, and not sons” (Heb 12:8). Paul guards against forged letters: be not shaken “by spirit, nor by word, nor by letter as from us” (2Th 2:2), and supplies a mark of authenticity: “The salutation of Paul with mine own hand, which is the token in every epistle: so I write” (2Th 3:17); “ye see how large a letter I have written unto you with mine own hand” (Gal 6:11). And Peter warns that the counterfeit will arise from within: “there shall be false teachers among you, who privily shall bring in damnable heresies” (2Pe 2:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines spurious as not genuine; false; adulterate; not proceeding from the true source; and, of birth, not legitimate; bastard.
webster_full: SPURIOUS, a. Not genuine; not proceeding from the true source, or from the source pretended; counterfeit; false; adulterate.
Spurious writings are such as are not composed by the authors to whom they are ascribed.
2. Not legitimate; bastard; as spurious issue.
scriptures: Heb 12:8
But if ye be without chastisement, whereof all are partakers, then are ye bastards, and not sons.
That ye be not soon shaken in mind, or be troubled, neither by spirit, nor by word, nor by letter as from us, as that the day of Christ is at hand.
The salutation of Paul with mine own hand, which is the token in every epistle: so I write.
Gal 6:11
Ye see how large a letter I have written unto you with mine own hand.

But there were false prophets also among the people, even as there shall be false teachers among you, who privily shall bring in damnable heresies, even denying the Lord that bought them, and bring upon themselves swift destruction.
corruption_summary: The test of genuineness is sought in feeling or profession, and Hebrews points to chastening.
corruption_paragraphs: Hebrews 12:8 is one of the most consoling verses in Scripture for anyone under God's discipline, and it is almost never read that way. The argument runs backwards from what everyone assumes: the son who is chastened is proved a son, and the man who never is has reason for concern. If ye endure chastening, God dealeth with you as with sons; for what son is he whom the father chasteneth not? Discipline is presented as the evidence of legitimacy, which turns a believer's hardest seasons into an argument for his standing rather than against it.

The other sense of the word bears on the canon, and Paul's practice is instructive. He assumed forged letters would circulate under his name — 2 Thessalonians 2:2 shows one had already unsettled that church — and his answer was not anxiety but a mark: the salutation in his own hand, the token in every epistle. The early church applied the same instinct on a larger scale, and the books it received were the ones with apostolic descent, which is what a canon is. The Reformation's appeal to Scripture depends on that discrimination having been made carefully, and it was.

Second Peter 2:1 is the reminder that counterfeits are an inside problem: false teachers among you, bringing in heresies privily. The spurious thing rarely announces itself as a rival; it presents as the genuine article with better credentials, and it establishes itself inside a congregation's trust before anyone examines its parentage. The remedy in both senses of the word is the same test: descent. Where did this come from? A doctrine, like a letter and like a son, is authenticated by its origin.
roots_summary: Greek nothos (G3541), illegitimate, a bastard; huios (G5207), son; semeion (G4592), a token, sign; pseudodidaskalos (G5572), a false teacher.
roots_lines: Greek nothos (G3541) — illegitimate, bastard; Hebrews 12:8 only.
Greek semeion (G4592) — token, mark; 2 Thessalonians 3:17 — the token in every epistle.
Greek pseudodidaskaloi (G5572) — false teachers; 2 Peter 2:1 only.
usage: “Then are ye bastards, and not sons” — and the chastened one is the son.
“Nor by letter as from us” — forgeries were already circulating.
“False teachers among you… privily” — it is an inside problem.

pos: n. (censorious speech; reproach cast on a name; the state of being spoken against)
etymology: Latin obloquium, from ob-, against, and loqui, to speak — a speaking against. It is the ordinary weather of the Christian's public life, and the New Testament treats it as such.
biblical_def: Obloquy is being spoken against. The Jews at Rome say of the Christian faith, “as concerning this sect, we know that every where it is spoken against” (Act 28:22). Paul reports it as his ordinary condition: “being defamed, we intreat: we are made as the filth of the world, and are the offscouring of all things unto this day” (1Co 4:13). David knows it: “I have heard the slander of many: fear was on every side” (Psa 31:13). The Lord makes it a beatitude when it is false and for His sake (Mat 5:11). And Peter turns it into evidence: “If ye be reproached for the name of Christ, happy are ye; for the spirit of glory and of God resteth upon you” (1Pe 4:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines obloquy as censorious speech; reproachful language; language that casts contempt on men or their actions; and cause of reproach; disgrace.
webster_full: OBLOQUY, n. Censorious speech; reproachful language; language that casts contempt on men or their actions.
Shall names that made your city the glory of the earth, be censured and defamed in the obloquy of a few?
2. Cause of reproach; disgrace.
scriptures: But we desire to hear of thee what thou thinkest: for as concerning this sect, we know that every where it is spoken against.
Being defamed, we intreat: we are made as the filth of the world, and are the offscouring of all things unto this day.
For I have heard the slander of many: fear was on every side: while they took counsel together against me, they devised to take away my life.
Mat 5:11
Blessed are ye, when men shall revile you, and persecute you, and shall say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake.
If ye be reproached for the name of Christ, happy are ye; for the spirit of glory and of God resteth upon you: on their part he is evil spoken of, but on your part he is glorified.
corruption_summary: Being spoken against is taken as proof of faithfulness, and Peter attaches conditions to the comfort.
corruption_paragraphs: The comfort is real and it is conditional, and both halves must be kept. First Peter 4:14 promises the spirit of glory to those reproached for the name of Christ, and the very next verse removes the loophole: but let none of you suffer as a murderer, or as a thief, or as an evildoer, or as a busybody in other men's matters. The last item is the pointed one. A Christian may attract genuine hostility by interfering, by rudeness, by a manner that has nothing of Christ in it, and then claim the beatitude — and Peter names that exact case and excludes it.

The opposite error is to treat all obloquy as a signal that something has gone wrong. Acts 28:22 records the faith being everywhere spoken against at the outset, before any Christian had done anything to deserve it, and 1 Corinthians 4:13 has an apostle describing himself as the offscouring of all things. A church whose reputation is uniformly good among people who reject its Lord should ask what it has stopped saying. The gospel names sin, claims exclusivity and calls for repentance, and there is no arrangement of tone that makes those universally welcome.

Between the two errors lies the discipline of not answering. Paul's phrase in 1 Corinthians 4:13 is being defamed, we intreat — and the pattern beneath it is 1 Peter 2:23, who when He was reviled, reviled not again, but committed Himself to Him that judgeth righteously. That is not passivity; it is a transfer of the case to a court with better evidence. A man's name is one of the things he may hand over, and the last verdict on it will not be delivered by the people currently discussing him.
roots_summary: Greek antilego (G483), to speak against; dusphemeo (G1425), to defame; oneidizo (G3679), to reproach; perikatharma / peripsema (G4027, G4067), filth, offscouring.
roots_lines: Greek antilegetai (G483) — it is spoken against; Acts 28:22, Luke 2:34, Titus 1:9, 2:9.
Greek dusphemoumenoi (G1425) — being defamed; 1 Corinthians 4:13 only.
Greek oneidizo (G3679) — to reproach; 1 Peter 4:14, Matthew 5:11, Romans 15:3.
usage: “Every where it is spoken against” — said of the faith at the outset.
“Being defamed, we intreat” — and the case is transferred, not argued.
“Let none of you suffer… as a busybody” — the loophole Peter closes.

pos: n. (the seizing of goods by violence; plunder taken openly and by force)
etymology: Latin rapina, from rapere, to seize — the root of rapacious and ravening. The AV's usual words are ravening, robbery and spoil.
biblical_def: Rapine is violent seizure. God says of Himself, “For I the LORD love judgment, I hate robbery for burnt offering” (Isa 61:8) — plunder does not become acceptable by being given to Him. Ezekiel indicts a whole population: “The people of the land have used oppression, and exercised robbery, and have vexed the poor and needy” (Eze 22:29). Amos says they “store up violence and robbery in their palaces” (Amo 3:10). The Lord finds it inside religion: “your inward part is full of ravening and wickedness” (Luk 11:39). And the persecuted took the loss with joy, “knowing in yourselves that ye have in heaven a better and an enduring substance” (Heb 10:34).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines rapine as the act of plundering; the seizing and carrying away of things by force; and violence, force.
webster_full: RAPINE, n. The act of plundering; the seizing and carrying away of things by force.
2. Violence; force.
RAPACIOUS, a. Given to plunder; disposed or accustomed to seize by violence; seizing by force.
RAPACITY, n. Addictedness to plunder; the exercise of plunder; ravenousness.
scriptures: Isa 61:8
For I the LORD love judgment, I hate robbery for burnt offering; and I will direct their work in truth, and I will make an everlasting covenant with them.
The people of the land have used oppression, and exercised robbery, and have vexed the poor and needy: yea, they have oppressed the stranger wrongfully.
Amo 3:10
For they know not to do right, saith the LORD, who store up violence and robbery in their palaces.
And the Lord said unto him, Now do ye Pharisees make clean the outside of the cup and the platter; but your inward part is full of ravening and wickedness.
For ye had compassion of me in my bonds, and took joyfully the spoiling of your goods, knowing in yourselves that ye have in heaven a better and an enduring substance.
corruption_summary: Plunder is laundered through religion or through legality, and the prophets refuse both routes.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 61:8 closes the religious route in nine words: I hate robbery for burnt offering. The offering was the most sacred use to which property could be put, and God says it does not sanctify what was taken. This is one of the recurring themes of the prophets — that worship funded by injustice is not worship God receives — and it applies wherever generosity is used to settle an account that repentance and restitution should settle. Zacchaeus is the model of the alternative: half his goods to the poor, and fourfold restoration to anyone he had defrauded, in that order and with the restitution named specifically.

The legal route is the one Amos and Ezekiel attack, and it is the more common. Ezekiel 22 is a catalogue of a society's institutions failing in sequence — princes, priests, prophets, and then the people of the land, who have used oppression and exercised robbery and vexed the poor and needy. None of it required a mask or a weapon. It was done through the ordinary operation of contracts, courts and wages by men who would have been offended to be called robbers, and God's word for it is the word used of highwaymen.

Luke 11:39 moves the charge inside, and to a religious audience: the Pharisees make clean the outside of the cup and the platter, and the inward part is full of ravening and wickedness. The word is the one used of a wolf. That is the Lord's assessment of scrupulous men whose scruples never reached their acquisitions. Hebrews 10:34 gives the other side and it is the only real defence against the fear of loss: they took joyfully the spoiling of their goods, knowing they had a better and an enduring substance. A man who knows where his estate actually is can be robbed and not be poor.
roots_summary: Hebrew gazel (H1498), robbery, violent seizure; shod (H7701), spoil, devastation; ashaq (H6231), to oppress, defraud; Greek harpage (G724), ravening, extortion.
roots_lines: Hebrew gazel (H1498) — robbery, that which is seized; Isaiah 61:8, Ezekiel 22:29, Leviticus 6:4.
Hebrew ashaq (H6231) — to oppress, defraud; Ezekiel 22:29, Leviticus 19:13, Micah 2:2, Malachi 3:5.
Greek harpage (G724) — ravening, plunder, extortion; Luke 11:39, Matthew 23:25, Hebrews 10:34.
usage: “I hate robbery for burnt offering” — the religious route, closed in nine words.
“The people of the land have used oppression” — and it was all lawful.
“Took joyfully the spoiling of your goods” — knowing where the estate actually is.
